claim: Most tools used to evaluate scientific excellence are biased in favour of established disciplines and against interdisciplinary research.
source: When making decisions about funding and jobs the scientific community should recognise that most of the tools used to evaluate scientific excellence are biased in favour of established disciplines and against interdisciplinary research.
evidence: This is the main thesis statement of the manuscript, supported by subsequent arguments and data about ERC grant success rates and structural features of scientific communities.

claim: The success rate for interdisciplinary applications to ERC Advanced Grants and ERC Starting Grants has been lower than the success rate for single-discipline applications in each of the first four years of these schemes.
source: Although excellence is the sole selection criterion used to award these grants, the success rate for applications categorised as interdisciplinary has been lower than the success rate for single-discipline applications in each of the first four years of these schemes (Labastida, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Labastida, 2013, which provides empirical data on ERC grant success rates.

claim: Excellence is the sole selection criterion used to award ERC Advanced Grants and ERC Starting Grants.
source: Although excellence is the sole selection criterion used to award these grants, the success rate for applications categorised as interdisciplinary has been lower than the success rate for single-discipline applications in each of the first four years of these schemes (Labastida, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about ERC grant criteria, supported by citation to Labastida, 2013.

claim: Objective measures of bias against interdisciplinary research are very difficult to come by.
source: Such objective measures of the bias against interdisciplinary research are very difficult to come by, yet subjective and/or personal experiences are commonplace.
evidence: This is an assertion about the availability of objective measures, based on the author's assessment of the research landscape.

claim: Subjective and/or personal experiences of bias against interdisciplinary research are commonplace.
source: Such objective measures of the bias against interdisciplinary research are very difficult to come by, yet subjective and/or personal experiences are commonplace.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about the prevalence of subjective experiences.

claim: Research outside of well-established disciplines is commonly rejected outright by journal editors as uninteresting to the community.
source: It seems a common occurrence for research outside of the well-established disciplines to be rejected outright by journal editors as uninteresting to the community.
evidence: This is presented as a common occurrence based on the author's observation and experience.

claim: Journal editors may have difficulties finding referees who have the expertise needed to review interdisciplinary papers.
source: Furthermore, even if a submitted manuscript passes the initial screen, the editor may have difficulties finding referees who have the expertise needed to review the paper.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of interdisciplinary research spanning multiple fields.

claim: Department heads and programme managers face a zero-sum struggle for resources.
source: And when it comes to nourishing particular disciplines, those in positions of power—such as department heads in universities or programme managers at funding agencies—face the daily grind of a zero-sum struggle for resources.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about resource allocation in academic institutions.

claim: Department heads and programme managers are often only able or willing to support interdisciplinary research if doing so does not erode resources available to researchers in their particular discipline.
source: This means that they are often only able or willing to support interdisciplinary research with lab space or research grants if doing so does not erode the resources available to researchers working in that particular discipline.
evidence: This is presented as a consequence of the zero-sum resource struggle.

claim: The zero-sum resource struggle inevitably tips the scales against researchers who do not fit comfortably into any existing discipline.
source: This inevitably tips the scales against researchers who do not fit comfortably into any existing discipline.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of the resource allocation dynamics described.

claim: Most researchers work in dense scientific communities.
source: Most researchers work in what could be termed 'dense scientific communities'.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about the structure of scientific communities.

claim: In dense scientific communities, members attend the same meetings, publish in the same journals, cite each other's papers and often collaborate and compete with each other.
source: By this I mean well-established scientific communities in which the different members attend the same meetings, publish in the same journals, cite each other's papers and often collaborate and compete with each other.
evidence: This is the author's definition of dense scientific communities based on observable characteristics.

claim: In dense scientific communities, the goals of the field are well defined and well known.
source: In such dense scientific communities, the goals of the field are well defined and well known, and are addressed simultaneously by many scientists in a competitive way, much like an Olympic race.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of dense scientific communities.

claim: In dense scientific communities, goals are addressed simultaneously by many scientists in a competitive way, much like an Olympic race.
source: In such dense scientific communities, the goals of the field are well defined and well known, and are addressed simultaneously by many scientists in a competitive way, much like an Olympic race.
evidence: This is an analogy used to describe the competitive nature of research in dense communities.

claim: In dense scientific communities, the preferred venues for publication of new results are widely recognised.
source: Moreover, in such communities the preferred venues for the publication of new results—high-impact journals in some communities, competitive conferences in others—are also widely recognised and community members are more than willing to review manuscripts written by their colleagues, because it helps them to stay on top of the competition and to be inspired by yet-unpublished research.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of dense scientific communities.

claim: Community members in dense scientific communities are willing to review manuscripts written by their colleagues because it helps them stay on top of the competition and be inspired by yet-unpublished research.
source: Moreover, in such communities the preferred venues for the publication of new results—high-impact journals in some communities, competitive conferences in others—are also widely recognised and community members are more than willing to review manuscripts written by their colleagues, because it helps them to stay on top of the competition and to be inspired by yet-unpublished research.
evidence: This explains the motivation for peer review participation in dense communities.

claim: Publications in dense scientific communities get cited quite rapidly and in large numbers by many peers working in the same area.
source: Publications in such communities also get cited quite rapidly and in large numbers, by the many peers working in the same area.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of citation patterns in dense communities.

claim: In dense scientific communities, the 'elders' are well recognised and have the authority to set the rules by which excellence is measured.
source: In dense scientific communities, the 'elders' are well recognised and have the authority to set the rules by which excellence in this community is measured.
evidence: This describes the hierarchical structure and authority in dense communities.

claim: Elders in dense scientific communities are forthcoming with letters of recommendation for their best intellectual offspring.
source: These elders are also forthcoming with letters of recommendation for their best intellectual offspring.
evidence: This describes a support mechanism available in dense communities.

claim: Young researchers who successfully address problems deemed important by elders in dense communities are rewarded handsomely.
source: Young researchers who play by the rules and successfully address problems that have been deemed important by the elders are rewarded handsomely and, over time, these young researchers become elders themselves, thus ensuring that the community continues to flourish.
evidence: This describes the reward system in dense scientific communities.

claim: Young researchers in dense communities eventually become elders themselves, ensuring that the community continues to flourish.
source: Young researchers who play by the rules and successfully address problems that have been deemed important by the elders are rewarded handsomely and, over time, these young researchers become elders themselves, thus ensuring that the community continues to flourish.
evidence: This describes the self-perpetuating nature of dense scientific communities.

claim: Genuine interdisciplinary research is nothing like a competitive race.
source: Genuine interdisciplinary research is nothing like a competitive race.
evidence: This contrasts interdisciplinary research with the competitive nature of dense communities.

claim: Interdisciplinary research is much more like a solitary exploratory hike through an uncharted landscape.
source: It is much more like a solitary exploratory hike through an uncharted landscape.
evidence: This is an analogy used to characterize interdisciplinary research.

claim: In interdisciplinary research, there are no community elders to give guidance, define and rank important research goals, or write recommendation letters.
source: There are no community elders to give guidance, to define and rank the important research goals, or to write recommendation letters to their intellectual offspring.
evidence: This describes the lack of community support structures in interdisciplinary research.

claim: In interdisciplinary research, there are no peers to compete with or use as reviewers.
source: There are no peers to compete with or use as reviewers; and there are no community-specific journals or conferences.
evidence: This describes the isolation of interdisciplinary researchers.

claim: In interdisciplinary research, there are no community-specific journals or conferences.
source: There are no peers to compete with or use as reviewers; and there are no community-specific journals or conferences.
evidence: This describes the lack of publication venues specific to interdisciplinary research.

claim: The intricate and encompassing community support structure present in dense scientific communities is completely missing in interdisciplinary research.
source: In general, the intricate and encompassing community support structure present in dense scientific communities is completely missing.
evidence: This summarizes the structural disadvantages of interdisciplinary research.

claim: Many objective measures used to assess researchers—such as impact factors, citation counts, or letters of recommendation—are highly biased in favour of researchers in dense scientific communities.
source: All this means that many of the so-called 'objective measures' that are used to assess researchers—such as impact factors (with all their flaws), citation counts, or letters of recommendation—are highly biased in favour of researchers who belong to dense scientific communities at the expense of those who are members of sparse scientific communities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural differences between dense and sparse communities.

claim: Recognising excellence at and between the boundaries of established disciplines is difficult.
source: Although recognising excellence at and between the boundaries of established disciplines is difficult, it is essential that we keep trying to identify scientists who have the potential to make real breakthroughs in these areas.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in evaluating interdisciplinary research.

claim: It is essential to keep trying to identify scientists who have the potential to make real breakthroughs at and between the boundaries of established disciplines.
source: Although recognising excellence at and between the boundaries of established disciplines is difficult, it is essential that we keep trying to identify scientists who have the potential to make real breakthroughs in these areas.
evidence: This is a normative claim about the importance of supporting interdisciplinary research.

claim: If interdisciplinary scientists are not identified and funded, certain highly promising interdisciplinary areas might remain unexplored because no one else is working in them.
source: If these scientists are not identified and funded, then—almost by definition—certain highly promising interdisciplinary areas might remained unexplored because no one else is working in them.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the sparse nature of interdisciplinary research communities.

claim: In dense scientific communities, if we fail to recognise and support the very best person working towards a particular important goal, someone else will probably reach the same goal, albeit with some delay.
source: This is not a problem in dense scientific communities: if we fail to recognise and support the very best person working towards a particular important goal in this field, then someone else will probably reach the same goal, albeit with some delay.
evidence: This describes the redundancy in dense scientific communities.

claim: The progress of science in dense communities is relatively unaffected if we fail to support the very best person working towards a particular goal.
source: Unfair as it may be, the progress of science is relatively unaffected by such an outcome.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the redundancy in dense communities.

claim: Excellence in interdisciplinary research should be actively sought, identified and rewarded even more than excellence in dense communities.
source: Hence, as rare as excellence may be in the outback of interdisciplinary research, it should be actively sought, identified and rewarded even more than excellence in dense communities.
evidence: This is a normative recommendation based on the unique value of interdisciplinary research.

claim: The three tools most widely used to evaluate researchers—measures based on impact factors, citation counts and recommendation letters—are highly biased in favour of members in dense communities.
source: First we must recognise that the three tools that are most widely used to evaluate researchers—measures based on impact factors, citation counts and recommendation letters—are highly biased in favour of members in dense communities.
evidence: This reiterates the main claim about bias in evaluation tools.

claim: 'Over-ambitious' is a code-word used for rejecting interdisciplinary grant proposals.
source: For example, one code-word used for rejecting interdisciplinary grant proposals is 'over-ambitious'.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about grant review practices.

claim: 'Over-ambitious' often stands for saying that the scientist intends to do something radically different from what has been done until now and does not follow the 'rules' of the reviewer's home scientific community.
source: This often stands for saying that the scientist intends to do something that is radically different from what has been done until now and does not follow the 'rules' of the reviewer's home scientific community.
evidence: This interprets the meaning behind the 'over-ambitious' label.

claim: The predictability of a scientific endeavour is arguably inversely proportional to how innovative it is.
source: Besides, the predictability of a scientific endeavour is arguably inversely proportional to how innovative it is.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about innovation and predictability.

claim: Any scientific project that is not 'over-ambitious' is by definition not innovative enough.
source: So maybe any scientific project that is not 'over-ambitious' is by definition not innovative enough?
evidence: This is presented as a rhetorical question suggesting a relationship between ambition and innovation.

claim: An objective measure of the density of various scientific communities could be taken into account when making decisions about funding and jobs.
source: A useful countermeasure would be to develop an objective measure of the density of various scientific communities that could be taken into account when making decisions about funding and jobs.
evidence: This is a proposed solution to correct bias against interdisciplinary research.

claim: If two scientists are judged equal on standard measures, the scientist from the less dense community could be ranked higher to compensate for biases.
source: If two scientists are judged equal on the basis of the standard measures, then the scientist from the less dense community (see figure) could be ranked higher to compensate for the biases against researchers in these areas.
evidence: This is a proposed method for correcting bias, with reference to the figure illustrating network density.

claim: The social network of a scientist consists of all the scientists cited by or citing that scientist, with edges connecting those scientists who have cited each other.
source: The social network of a particular scientist, say Mary Smith (red circle), consists of all the scientists (blue circles) cited by Mary or citing Mary, with edges connecting those scientists who have cited each other.
evidence: This defines how to construct a scientist's social network, as illustrated in the figure.

claim: A scientist's network will lie somewhere between two extremes: a maximally dense network in which all scientists cite each other, and a maximally sparse network in which there are no citations among scientists except citations by or to the focal scientist.
source: The resulting network will lie somewhere between two extremes: a maximally dense network (right), in which all the scientists in the network cite each other, and a maximally sparse network (left) in which there are no citations among the scientists except citations by or to Mary.
evidence: This describes the spectrum of network density illustrated in the figure.

claim: Dense scientific communities that receive very little input from and exert very little influence over other fields of science could be identified through sophisticated analysis.
source: For example, it would be useful to identify dense scientific communities that receive very little input from, and exert very little influence over, other fields of science; decisions to fund such 'mutual-admiration societies' should be subject to higher than usual levels of scrutiny.
evidence: This proposes using network analysis to identify insular communities.

claim: Decisions to fund 'mutual-admiration societies' should be subject to higher than usual levels of scrutiny.
source: For example, it would be useful to identify dense scientific communities that receive very little input from, and exert very little influence over, other fields of science; decisions to fund such 'mutual-admiration societies' should be subject to higher than usual levels of scrutiny.
evidence: This is a normative recommendation about funding decisions.

claim: Scientists who have integrated two previously unrelated areas of research to open up completely new fields of inquiry could be identified by network analysis.
source: Conversely, scientists who have integrated two previously unrelated areas of research to open up completely new fields of inquiry could also be identified by such an analysis, and recognised accordingly.
evidence: This proposes using network analysis to identify bridging scientists.

claim: More research should be devoted to measuring the density of scientific communities, probably based on various techniques from graph theory.
source: More research should be devoted to measuring the density of scientific communities (probably based on various techniques from graph theory), and more thought should be given as to how this measure can be factored into the evaluation of scientific excellence.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: More thought should be given as to how the measure of community density can be factored into the evaluation of scientific excellence.
source: More research should be devoted to measuring the density of scientific communities (probably based on various techniques from graph theory), and more thought should be given as to how this measure can be factored into the evaluation of scientific excellence.
evidence: This is a recommendation for improving evaluation practices.

claim: Correction for community density is not intended to compensate an interdisciplinary scientist for personal hardships.
source: Let me be clear, however: any such correction is not intended to compensate an interdisciplinary scientist for his or her personal hardships.
evidence: This clarifies the purpose of the proposed correction.

claim: Correction for community density is needed to prevent seemingly objective evaluation tools from misleading us and holding back scientific progress.
source: Rather, such a correction is needed to prevent seemingly objective evaluation tools from misleading us and, as a result, holding back scientific progress by diverting funds and jobs from people who have the potential to perform truly ground-breaking science.
evidence: This explains the rationale for correcting bias in evaluation tools.

claim: Without correction, evaluation tools may divert funds and jobs from people who have the potential to perform truly ground-breaking science.
source: Rather, such a correction is needed to prevent seemingly objective evaluation tools from misleading us and, as a result, holding back scientific progress by diverting funds and jobs from people who have the potential to perform truly ground-breaking science.
evidence: This describes the negative consequence of biased evaluation tools.
